catalog_quote: [p. 257] The word can be defined as the stress bearing unit (stress group). As to distribution of the stress within the word see section 10. [...] [p. 279] Legbó has three tonemes as can be shown for nouns as follows: [...] [p. 280] Stress. Stress is not phonemic. new_statements.rule_in_words: Legbo is a three-tone language (H, M, L). Word stress is non-contrastive and fully predictable from tone: within the phonological word (1-6 syllables), stress falls on the syllable bearing the highest tone; if several syllables tie for highest tone, the rightmost of them (nearest the word end) is stressed.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the authors note that mid tone and stress are not marked in their transcription (p. 256). A separate word-level 'tenseness' feature (fortis, lengthened consonant with compensatory vowel shortening) is phonemic but is treated apart from stress (pp. 280-282).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the phonological word ('stress group', 1-6 syllables, potential pause on either side), which 'largely corresponds to the word unit in the grammatical hierarchy' (p. 257). Utterance-level prominence (raised first syllable, decrescendo, final pitch drop) is described separately (pp. 257-258). Description is of the Adadama dialect, fieldwork 1964-66.
new_statements.identity_note: Spreda & Spreda (1966) call the language 'Legbó' and the people/clan 'Agbó' (= Glottolog legb1242 Legbo, ISO agb, also spelled Leggbo in Hyman/Udoh/Paster's work); their statement explicitly describes the Adadama dialect (one of four township dialects: Igbo Ekureku, Igbo Imabana, Adadama, Itigidi; Glottolog lists no subdialect codes). The Hyman/Udoh/Paster materials are based on Imelda Udoh as consultant (Berkeley field methods 2001-02).

tone_statements.quote: There are three level tones – (H)igh, (M)id and (L)ow tones generally. All tones ... to form contours. This three-way contrast operates in noun roots, although their ... may bear either mid or low tones. (3a) MH lɛdʒál 'sacrifice' ... However, there is only a two way contrast in verb roots. M tone verbs and L tone verbs. There are two classes of verbs. The first has a M tone, while the second has either a H or L tone on the root, and its choice is determined by the grammar.
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L; contours are combinations. Noun roots 3-way, prefixes M or L; verb roots M vs L(~H). p.578: mid unmarked, H ´ L ` HL ˆ LH ˇ. Two margin-cut words elided; no stress.

tone_statements.citation: Hyman, Larry M. & Imelda Udoh. 2003. Tone mapping in Leggbo. Frankfurter Afrikanistische Blätter 15: 121-139 (special issue 'Stress and Tone - the African Experience', ed. Rose-Juliet Anyanwu). Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
tone_statements.quote: In the preceding sections we have documented the tonal properties of Leggbó. We saw first that H, M and L tones are lexically contrastive on nouns, whereas verb roots show only a binary tonal opposition, which we characterized as /L/ vs. /M/. Whether these roots tones will be realized as L, M or H depends on the various combinations of inflectional features ... 297 out of 326, or 91% of the monosyllabic noun stems, carry one of the three level tones H, M or L. This suggests strongly that there is a tendency to have one tone per tone-bearing unit (TBU).
tone_statements.locator: §4 Conclusion, ms p. 12; second part §2 Noun tones (i), ms p. 4
tone_statements.summary: Three level tones H, M, L contrastive on nouns; verb roots /L/ vs /M/ plus M or L suffix tone give melodies (HM MM ML LM LL, LHM) mapped left to right by syllable; floating L prefix; H/M fall at pause.
